title: The Lever — Who Holds the Throttle

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the twenty-first of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [excited] Claire, what's leading?
Three things. Israel bombed a Syrian runway to keep Turkey off it — and this time Washington rebuked Israel, not the men it hit.
The chips finally cross into China — and it turns out Beijing, not Washington, is holding the throttle now.
And a hobby where the most expensive thing you can buy is not the thing that decides how good it looks. Home cinema.
[curious] The room beats the box. Okay. Start with the runway.
Before dawn on Tuesday, Israeli warplanes put eight strikes into the runway at Abu al-Duhur, an airbase in Idlib, in northwest Syria — about seventy kilometres from the Turkish border.
[curious] Why that base? What's special about it?
Its landlord. The post-Assad government in Damascus had lined it up for rehabilitation — with Turkey, its main military patron, doing the work.
So Israel bombs to stop a Turkish deployment before it can happen.
That's the stated reason. And the timing is the story: it landed eleven days after a brand-new defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
[thoughtful] A pact eleven days old, and someone's already testing whether it means anything.

Exactly that. It's an Article-Five-style arrangement — an attack on one treated as an attack on all — building on a Saudi-Pakistani accord from last year. Assad fell back in December, remember, and Turkey stepped in as the new government's patron.
So a new bloc is hardening, and Israel just poked it.
And the framings split hard. The wire read leads on the mechanics — and on how rare it is for Washington to publicly rebuke Israel.
Did they? Actually rebuke it?
The US ambassador to Ankara called the strike an unnecessary escalation. Qatar, Egypt and Saudi Arabia condemned it too.
And the view from Doha — Al Jazeera?
Israel as the aggressor, puncturing a fragile post-Assad order. From Beijing, Xinhua ran it cooler — two American allies carving Syria into spheres while Washington can't control either.
[wry] Which is its own little argument about American decline.
Here's the sceptic, though. The reason is disputed at the source. Both Ankara and Damascus deny any Turkish troops were deploying at all.
So if there's no evidence of a buildup —
— then the justification collapses into pretext. Some analysts read it as a warning shot, meant to deflate that new pact. And so far, Turkey has absorbed the strike without firing back.
[exhales] Hold that thought. Because there's a second version of the same move waiting in the money block, isn't there.
There is. Let's do the money. The dominant force this week wasn't the Federal Reserve. It was debt management.
Meaning what, in plain terms?
The thirty-year Treasury yield spiked to five point three four per cent — a nineteen-year high. So the Treasury at least doubled its buybacks and pushed it back down, under five point two.
[skeptical] Wait — the government reached in and set the price of its own debt?
That's exactly what a buyback does. It's a yield curve being administered, not discovered. And the dollar noticed first — the dollar index slid to a three-month low, near ninety-eight point eight.
[skeptical] Because markets read it as, what, quietly printing money?
As mildly debasement-friendly, yes. And here's the diagnostic that matters for anyone holding a portfolio: on the day, stocks and bonds fell together.
Which means a balanced book got no cushion at all.

None. Gold sat near a record — around four thousand four hundred and eighty-one dollars — driven by the soft dollar and central-bank buying, not by real yields. Bitcoin jumped about seven per cent, to roughly seventy-two thousand, on a regulatory push.
So what does it mean for the handful of things this desk actually watches?

A soft dollar flatters global equity, so a world-index fund sits near a record. Global bonds are propped by the buyback bid — fragile stability, not a rally. Gold and bitcoin both run with the liquidity. That's explanation, not advice.
[thoughtful] And the net between stocks and bonds is thin right now. What's the thing to watch?
Jackson Hole, on the twenty-eighth — a central-bank read colliding with a dollar already at three-month lows. Now, Singapore.
[deadpan] Go.
Sunday is the National Day Rally, and the government has pre-trailed the theme: the cost of raising a child. Childcare affordability.
That's a live nerve here.
It is. And underneath it, the trade number looked spectacular and was actually narrow. Exports up twenty-four point two per cent in July — but almost entirely artificial-intelligence electronics.
How narrow are we talking?

Strip out electronics and it's soft. Pharmaceuticals fell fifty-six point seven per cent in the same month. The boom is essentially one product line — and the sceptic says one product cycle separates boom from base effect.
[curious] Okay, the chips. This is the throttle story.
Right. After seven months in limbo, physical Nvidia H-two-hundreds are landing on the Chinese mainland. ByteDance and Tencent have each taken about ten thousand of them.
That sounds like a lot.
It's thirteen per cent of what each is licensed to buy. The interesting number is the small one — because the hand on the tap is now Beijing's.
Beijing is rationing its own access to American chips?

Its planning agency signs off every order, and is steering firms toward Huawei's own line instead. Washington wrote the licence — and even takes a twenty-five per cent cut of each sale — but Beijing decides how fast to be restrained.
[amused] So the country the controls were built to restrain is now the one applying the brakes. That's the exact shape of the Syria story.
It's the whole issue's shape. Quick one for your home lab, Theo — the open-weights frontier keeps getting bigger, and further out of reach of a desk.
Let me guess. The big new model doesn't fit.

Seven hundred and forty-three billion parameters. It needs a rack. What actually fits two of the top consumer cards is a smaller pair — a big open model that squeezes into sixty-odd gigabytes for reach, and a coder that punches above its size and leaves room for a long context.
And the headline benchmark on the big one — worth trusting?

[skeptical] Careful there. It leads on one cyber score, but on the offensive side it trails the closed models by more than twenty points. A single headline number is a poor way to buy a security tool.
Fair. The models worth running are the ones you can already run. Kit?
GoPro stopped making an action cube and built a pocket cinema camera. The Mission One Pro — a one-inch, fifty-megapixel sensor, shooting eight-K.
[excited] A real cinema sensor you clip to a bag?

Reviewers gave it a clean sweep of editor's-choice awards, which the action line never earned. It starts around four hundred and ninety-nine dollars if you pay the subscription, six hundred if you don't. The sceptic note: it's still a GoPro underneath — watch the sustained eight-K runtime, and the price leans on that subscription.
And the maker of the day — the Atelier. Ski gadgets, right?
Ski electronics. And the honest finding is that almost nothing on a mountain is bought once. The safety layer is a consumable.
How so?

An avalanche beacon should be retired at about ten years, even if it's barely been used — and you run fresh alkaline batteries, never lithium, because lithium lies about how much charge is left. The one genuine buy-once item is the airbag, and it's a white-label story: one Swiss firm builds the engine and sells the same heart into a dozen different badges.
[curious] And for someone flying to Japan every ski season — why does that matter?

Because the modern airbag runs on a supercapacitor. It flies as ordinary electronics — no paperwork. The old compressed-gas kind means airline notification, and in North America you fly the cylinder empty. Nine in ten buyers now pick electronic.
Same heart, different bag. So what's the line that ties it to everything else today?
[deadpan] Any device whose safety function depends on an app or a company's servers is a rental, not a purchase.
[laughs] There it is again. Control, in a hand you didn't suspect. Alright —
[warmly] Right. Take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[chuckles] Home cinema, Claire. Dedicated rooms. Projectors. And the great secret of the whole hobby.
Which is that the projector — the most expensive thing in the room — is not what decides how good it looks.
Then what does?
The room. The calibration. And the bass. There's a line the build threads repeat: your room and calibration beat any box — and a second subwoofer beats a better projector.
Who's on these build threads?

A measurement-obsessed crowd. The big forum runs multi-year build diaries where people set a target, measure, and verify they hit it. The ethos is that if you can measure it, you can fix it — and most people are chasing the wrong box.
[curious] So all the money spent on the shiny projector —

— is often the wrong lever. And the proof is what actually moved in twenty twenty-five. The projectors got a little better. The processors barely moved. The one genuine upgrade of the year was a piece of software.
Software? Not a thirty-thousand-dollar projector?
A firmware unlock called Active Room Treatment. Two hundred and ninety-nine dollars. It uses every speaker in the system to actively cancel the room's bass resonances.
[gasps] Three hundred dollars beats a thirty-three-thousand-dollar box.
For the thing most people get wrong, yes. Bass traps, a second subwoofer, and a proper calibration transform a system for a fraction of a new projector. That's the hobby's whole moral in one number.
And there's a lie in here somewhere — you flagged a streaming lie.

The lossless one. Your streaming service carries the Atmos badge, but it compresses the sound. The only way to get the real lossless track outside a disc is a dedicated movie server. People pay four thousand dollars for one, just for the audio.
What does it really cost to be in this world?

Entry is a few thousand. A serious room runs thirty to ninety thousand. A reference room, past a hundred and fifty. And here's the tell — forty to sixty per cent of the budget is construction. The room, not the boxes.
[thoughtful] And the sceptic's case? Because there's always one.

The existential threat to the projector itself. For most rooms — lit, multi-use — a twenty twenty-six flagship television, and now hundred-and-thirty-inch sets, genuinely beat a projector on brightness and punch.
[thoughtful] So the projector's last stand is a truly dark, dedicated room.
Build the room, or buy the giant television. The worst outcome is a flagship projector fighting a sunlit lounge.
[amused] The room is the machine. The box is just the box. Okay, I'm out of the hole. What's on culture?
A film opens wide today on a perfect score. Tony — an origin story of a young Anthony Bourdain, from A-twenty-four.
A hundred per cent on Rotten Tomatoes?

On about two dozen festival reviews. Dominic Sessa plays him, Antonio Banderas is the mentor. A perfect score on a small sample is a festival glow, not a verdict — the catch is the crowd verdict is still empty, and it opens against two studio tentpoles the same day.
[warmly] And music?
Chelsea Wolfe drops her ninth record the same day — The Dark. The doom-folk artist gone almost tender. The Guardian gave it an eighty, and heard her, in their words, cast off past toxic influences.
[warmly] On the wrist, anything?

A little indie oddity — a regatta chronograph for a race that never happened. The brand makes what they call imaginary vintage: faithful reissues of watches that never existed. A patented movement, ninety-nine pieces a colour.
[chuckles] A reissue of a thing that never was. I love that. And the body — family, fitness?
A clean one for parents. A new study of ten-to-thirteen-year-olds found the lever for a child's mind isn't the phone. It's the pillow.
Sleep over screens?

Sleep carried thirty-six per cent of the link between anxiety and school grades. Screen time — about six. It's a screen-time study that quietly demotes screens. And the practical move is dull but proven: the device off, not just on silent, in the last hour before bed.
[thoughtful] Guard the sleep. And fitness — the lazy person's win, please.
You'll like this. A review of eleven trials found that exercise snacks — bouts under five minutes, twice a day — genuinely lift fitness. Benefits from as little as four and a half minutes a week.
[laughs] Four and a half minutes a week. I can lose to that and still win.

The honest caveat: it raises fitness, not proven years. Do it because it's nearly free. And one for the diary — the Grand Prix here is Singapore's first-ever sprint weekend this year. Real points across three nights, not just Sunday.
And a table worth booking?

A starred chef loosening his tie — a second, cheaper restaurant from the man behind a Michelin one-star, a fifty-eight-dollar lunch. Over in Japan, the whole region hosts the Asian Games next month, if you want a reason to fly.
Alright — take us down slow, Claire. The Undercurrent.
[thoughtful] Kazakhstan. A country backing away from Moscow — while its phones walk the other way.
How do you mean, walk the other way?
Since twenty twenty-two, Astana has refused to endorse Russia's war, taken in the Russians who fled it, courted Western money. Its foreign policy leans west.
And the phones?

Google's share of Kazakh search fell from about eighty-nine per cent in twenty twenty-three to sixty-four in twenty twenty-five. Russia's Yandex climbed into the thirties. Its voice assistant is already on a million devices there.
[whispers] Nobody ordered that. No firewall.

That's what makes it unsettling. No decree, no ban on Google. Just a maps app with denser local coverage, a cheaper taxi, an assistant that speaks the language of the street. Each one a small, rational choice — and together, a country drifting. Sovereignty decided in the app store, not the cabinet.
Have we seen this before?

Russia's own path, a decade earlier. An antitrust ruling there in twenty fifteen, and by twenty eighteen Yandex had overtaken Google on Android at home. Kazakhstan is running the same arc — without even the ruling. Just the pull of the ecosystem.
Is it a clean Russian takeover, though?

No — and that's the honest part. The local fintech champion is homegrown and worth over sixteen billion dollars. A Chinese giant just bought a stake in it. It's a three-way contest — Russian, Chinese, and homegrown — and the one player quietly receding is the American one.
[thoughtful] Is the trend even real, or is it already cresting?

[drawn out] Good question — and the honest answer is, watch it. One later reading has the share slipping back. But the direction of three years isn't in dispute. And the line that stays with me is this: you can sanction a firewall. You cannot sanction convenience.
[exhales] The lever is the home screen. And someone else is holding it.
[warmly] The whole book, in one sentence. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
